newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Railway company seeks new deal with former Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Railway company seeks new deal with former Zaire.

text.p: Sizarail, the foreign-dominated company which ran the railways in the south and east of the former Zaire, has proposed a 30-year concession agreement with the new rulers of the country, the chief executive said on Wednesday.

Managing director Patrick Claes also told Reuters in an interview he expected an early end to the current dispute with the authorities in the new Democratic Republic of Congo, who unilaterally abrogated Sizarail's management contract soon after capturing the south last month.
As a side effect of the dispute, railway traffic across the Zambian border has stopped, freezing the region's copper exports through South African ports.

Claes, a Belgian national with 12 years of experience managing railways in Zaire, said Zambia acted because it did not have enough confidence in the new managers, the state's Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer Congolais (SNCC).
SNCC owes $3.3 million to Zambia Railways and $22 million to Spoornet, a partner in Sizarail -- part of a total debt of $650 million.
"When Sizarail was there, they were sure they would be paid -- it's a question of credibility," Claes said.
Spoornet representatives came to the southeastern capital Lubumbashi on April 24 and agreed to give up management.

Spoornet then demanded that SNCC give back all the South African rolling stock on its territory -- 14 locomotives, 100 freight wagons and 10 passenger carriages. SNCC refused, saying they needed them for internal traffic, Claes said.
"Now we have put some proposals. We propose to make a new company with a real concession for 30 years," he added.
"We are having no dialogue with these people... We hope that when there's a new government, we will talk," he said.
"Now they are beginning to understand that they made a mistake but they don't want to lose face."
In one sign of the way things are moving, the AFDL overruled a request by SNCC that Claes leave the country. Claes is awaiting developments in his company house in Lubumbashi.

The managing director said the concept of the 30-year concession was that Spoornet and the other partners in Sizarail would invest $400 million in the railway system and recoup the investment over the 30-year period.
This was the long-term ambition of the Sizarail partners when they signed the five-year management contract in 1995.
"The objective was to clean up the railway company and when we had shown the capacity of the management we would get loans and invest in the operation," Claes said.
If the new rulers do not come to terms with the Sizarail partners, Sizarail will sue for compensation, especially for a $20 million loan it took out from banks.
"The loan is a problem. We are in a case of force majeure. They have not observed the contract and we shall ask for compensation if we don't reach a new agreement with the alliance," said Claes.
